analysis.title: Can AI Grow the U.S. Out of Debt?
key_insights: MIM does not believe the U.S. or other countries can grow their way out of debt through an AI-driven productivity boost. AI will likely have at least some positive effect on measured productivity growth, but demographics and structural fiscal pressure outweigh it.

The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimates the U.S. would need average broad-based growth of 3.3% per year just to hold debt at 100% of GDP. Reducing deficits to 3% of GDP would need real growth averaging 4.4% over ten years.

The CBO's 2025 analysis puts average annual growth for 2023-2035 at 2.4% or higher in just 5% of simulated scenarios. The median estimate is 1.9%. The CBO treats sustained high real growth as a low-probability event.

Any AI boost to potential GDP growth has to offset, and eventually surpass, the drag from a shrinking labor force. Fiscal policy is described as an uphill battle because of growing non-discretionary obligations, rising interest payments and a lack of political will.

AI productivity gains depend on a favorable policy environment. U.S. AI development has benefited from global supply chains for cutting-edge chips, a large cluster of skilled researchers, and institutions that protect intellectual property.

China is the only other large economy MIM sees as able to roughly follow the U.S. path. Japan and Europe have much lower productivity growth plus their own demographic, fiscal and investment problems.
A fiscal improvement in the U.S. would likely lower yields globally, because most sovereign debt is still implicitly linked to U.S. Treasuries, and so could help other countries' indebtedness.
MIM's forecast is unchanged this month. It expects high headline inflation in 2026 because of the ongoing Iran conflict, and a significant decline in headline inflation in 2027 as oil prices fall.

MIM expects a Fed hike in December 2026 followed by another in Q1 2027, in line with market expectations. Yields are expected to stay high as markets focus on U.S. fiscal conditions, higher inflation and relatively strong growth.

MIM forecasts for the U.S.: GDP growth 2.2% in 2026 and 2.4% in 2027, December CPI y/y 4.0% in 2026 and 1.7% in 2027, 10-year Treasury yield 4.75% at end-2026 and 4.50% at end-2027, policy rate upper bound 4.25% and 4.50%, unemployment 4.3% in both years.

Risk 1: the Iran conflict. September CPI, PPI and import prices all showed significant effects from higher energy prices, and retail sales showed much higher nominal energy spending. If the inflation effect broadens, the Fed could raise rates more than expected, lifting both the policy rate and the 10-year outlook.

Risk 2: the AI boom has faced threats to its growth over recent quarters. Popular pushback against AI continues, and there are rising concerns about the business models that support valuations and the level of borrowing. Some growth may return depending on the November election outcomes.

risk_factors: Iran conflict keeps energy prices high and may broaden inflation, forcing more Fed hikes than expected.
AI boom growth threats: popular pushback, concerns over business models supporting valuations, and the level of borrowing.

Lack of political will to address structural fiscal issues.
Uncertain timing and magnitude of AI productivity gains.
geopolitical: The Iran conflict continues and has lasted longer than MIM expected, keeping energy prices and headline inflation elevated through 2026.

tension_points.bull_case: AI productivity improvements could raise expected potential GDP for some time, which would help growth-based deficit reduction.
tension_points.bear_case: The boost would have to be unprecedented in size and duration to offset a shrinking labor force and worsening fiscal obligations. The CBO sees growth of 2.4% or more in only 5% of scenarios, against 3.3% to 4.4% needed.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Productivity growth sustained well above CBO projections, enough to lift average real growth toward the 3.3% to 4.4% the CRFB says is needed.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI productivity gains must offset a shrinking labor force and worsening fiscal position, and the chances of the consistent high growth required are low.
theme_stances.evidence: chances of achieving the consistent high real growth required are low
